Color Theory. Color theory is the systematic study of how colors interact, combine, and affect perception and emotion. Far more than a practical guide to mixing pigments, it encompasses the physics of light, the psychology of human perception, and the conventions artists use to organize hues into harmonious relationships. Since the 17th century-particularly through scientists like Isaac Newton-color has been understood through frameworks of complementarity, temperature, and emotional association. Modern painters, from the Impressionists to Wassily Kandinsky, elevated color theory into a philosophical language. Primary, secondary, and tertiary colors form the foundational color wheel-a system for understanding relationships and mixtures. In addition, complementary colors (opposite on the wheel: red-green, blue-orange, yellow-purple) create maximum contrast and visual vibration when placed together. Similarly, color temperature divides the spectrum into warm (reds, yellows, oranges) and cool (blues, greens, purples) tones, affecting mood and spatial perception. Another important aspect is that saturation (or chroma) measures the intensity or purity of a hue, while value measures its lightness or darkness; both independent of hue itself. It's also worth knowing that kandinsky developed a systematic theory linking specific colors to emotional and spiritual states-red for passion, blue for spirituality, yellow for joy. Also worth noting is that paul Klee taught color theory at the Bauhaus and produced pedagogical works analyzing chromatic harmony and contrast. In addition, atmospheric perspective uses color desaturation and cooler tones to represent distant objects, exploiting how air affects color perception. Finally, the Impressionists revolutionized painting by treating color as independent of local object color and by juxtaposing pure hues rather than mixing them on the palette.
